section.title: Visions of Judgment
section.sectionRationale: The book shifts from sermons to a series of visions. The first two, devouring locusts and consuming fire, are met by the prophet's intercession, and twice the LORD relents. The third vision, the plumb line, is different: God will no longer pass by, for Israel has been measured against His standard and found crooked. Grace has a limit, and the third vision announces that the limit has come.
section.thesis: Twice the prophet's pleading stays the hand of God, showing how real and merciful His forbearance is; but the plumb line reveals a people measured against God's own uprightness and found so far out of true that judgment can no longer be turned aside.
section.frameNote: Three visions in ascending seriousness: the locusts that God relents from sending; the fire that God relents from sending; and the plumb line, where God declares He will spare Israel no longer.

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: He was preparing swarms of locusts just after the king’s harvest, as the late spring crop was coming up.
And when the locusts had eaten every green plant in the land, I said, “Lord GOD, please {{salach|forgive}}! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?”
So the LORD {{nacham|relented}} from this plan. “It will not happen,” He said.

units.label: The fire
units.note: the prophet pleads again, God relents

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: The Lord GOD was calling for judgment by fire. It consumed the great deep and devoured the land.
Then I said, “Lord GOD, please stop! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?”
So the LORD relented from this plan. “It will not happen either,” said the Lord GOD.
This is what He showed me: Behold, the Lord was standing by a wall true to plumb, with a {{anak|plumb line}} in His hand.
“Amos, what do you see?” asked the LORD. “A plumb line,” I replied. “Behold,” said the Lord, “I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel; I will no longer spare them:
The high places of Isaac will be deserted, and the sanctuaries of Israel will be laid waste; and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with My sword.”

salach.gloss: To forgive, pardon, a verb used in Scripture only of God, for forgiveness belongs to Him alone. Amos does not plead any merit in Israel; he simply cries salach, forgive, throwing the nation on God's mercy. The cry assumes that pardon is possible even when survival is not deserved, and that the God who threatens judgment is also the God who alone can forgive.

nacham.gloss: To relent, be moved to compassion, change a course of action, sometimes rendered repent in older versions. It does not mean God was mistaken or morally changed; it describes the LORD genuinely responding to intercession and withholding a threatened judgment. Twice the LORD nacham at the prophet's plea, showing that His warnings are real invitations to repentance and that mercy truly moves Him.

anak.gloss: A plumb line, or the tin or lead weight on a builder's cord used to test whether a wall is straight and true. God sets an anak among His people to show that Israel has been measured against His own uprightness and found badly out of true. A crooked wall that cannot be corrected must come down; the plumb line signals that the time for relenting has passed and judgment is just.

basic.context: Amos now receives a series of visions. In the first, God is about to send a plague of locusts to devour the crops; Amos begs Him to forgive, and God relents. In the second, God calls for a devastating fire; again Amos pleads, and again God relents. But the third vision is different: God stands by a wall with a plumb line, the builder's tool for testing whether a wall is straight. Israel has been measured against God's standard and found crooked, so God says He will spare them no longer.
basic.hermeneutics: These visions show two true things held together. First, God's forbearance is real: the prophet's intercession genuinely moves Him, and twice He holds back judgment. Second, mercy is not endless presumption: when a people are measured against God's own uprightness and refuse to be made straight, judgment finally comes, and it is just.
basic.originalLanguages: Amos cries salach, forgive, a verb used only of God. Twice the LORD nacham, relents, truly responding to the plea. Then God sets an anak, a plumb line, among His people, the builder's test for a true wall, and finds Israel crooked beyond correction.
basic.typology: Amos standing in the gap, pleading forgive, points to Christ, the true intercessor who does not merely ask for pardon but secures it by His own blood. The plumb line that condemns a crooked people anticipates the perfect standard fulfilled and satisfied in Christ, the one truly upright man.
basic.christ: Amos can only plead for mercy; Jesus is the mediator who obtains it, ever living to intercede for us. Where the plumb line exposes a wall too crooked to stand, Christ is the one life that is perfectly true to God's measure, and He bears the judgment the crooked deserve, so that in Him a fallen people can be rebuilt straight.
basic.god: God is astonishingly open to intercession, relenting twice at a single prophet's cry, which reveals a heart inclined to mercy. Yet He is also the righteous builder who will not let a hopelessly crooked wall stand forever. His patience is real, and so is the limit He sets on it.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 18 shows Abraham interceding and God willing to relent for the sake of a few. Exodus 32 records Moses pleading and the LORD relenting. Hebrews 7:25 presents Christ as the intercessor who always lives to save. 2 Peter 3:9 explains God's patience as space for repentance.

context.literary:
The five visions of Amos form a deliberate sequence, and Amos 7:1-9 holds the first three. Each opens with the same formula, 'This is what the Lord GOD showed me,' verses 1, 4 and 7, and the fourth will use it again at 8:1. They fall into two pairs. The first pair, locusts and fire, follow an identical pattern of threat, plea and reprieve, and even share their lines: 'How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?' appears word for word in verses 2 and 5, and the replies in verses 3 and 6 echo each other. The reader settles into a rhythm that suggests the pattern will go on.

The third vision breaks it in three ways. The prophet no longer speaks first; the LORD asks him, 'Amos, what do you see?' There is no plea from Amos and no reprieve. And the image is not a plague that arrives but a tool that measures. The change of tempo is the message: the LORD's patience has not ended in anger but in a decision. The fourth vision, the basket of summer fruit, 8:1-2, repeats the question and the formula, 'Amos, what do you see?' and adds 'I will no longer spare them,' the same words as verse 8 here, so verses 8 and 8:2 form a pair of verdicts bracketing the interruption in 7:10-17. The word-play of 8:2, in which the Hebrew for summer fruit sounds like the word for end, makes the same point in sound.

Within the visions the scale rises. Locusts strip the land, a natural disaster; fire consumes the 'great deep' and the land, a cosmic disaster; the plumb line is neither natural nor cosmic but moral and architectural, a standard laid against a wall. The first two are things happening to the nation, and the third is something done by God in the nation's midst, 'among My people Israel,' verse 8. The choice of images moves from what God can do to creation to what He will do with a people He has dwelt among.
context.historical:
Locusts were the great farming terror of the ancient Near East, and the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:38 and 28:42 name them. The prophet Joel would later describe four waves of them as 'My great army that I sent against you,' Joel 2:25. Amos places the swarm 'just after the king's harvest, as the late spring crop was coming up.' The king's share of the first cutting is probably in view, so that what was left for ordinary families was the later crop, the very thing that had to feed them until winter. If the locusts struck then, the people's own food would be gone, with no reserve. That explains why Amos cries that Jacob is 'so small.' This is a nation of small farmers on the edge.

The fire of verse 4 is harder to picture. It 'consumed the great deep,' a phrase that recalls the waters of the Flood, when 'all the fountains of the great deep burst forth,' Genesis 7:11. The details of the vision are symbolic, but a farming people might well hear in it a drought so severe that even the springs were gone. The effect is of the world itself failing.

The plumb line is a builder's tool, a weight on a cord used to check that a wall stands true. The image comes from the building trade at a time of great construction in Samaria, where the elite built stone houses, Amos 5:11, and ivory palaces, Amos 3:15. In the Old Testament a line and plummet could also be used for demolition, as when the LORD says He will stretch over Jerusalem 'the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab,' 2 Kings 21:13. Here, in the third vision, the plumb line is for testing and then for condemning.

The target in verse 9, 'the house of Jeroboam,' is Jeroboam II, who reigned forty-one years, 2 Kings 14:23. The sword rose against his house within a generation: his son Zechariah reigned six months before Shallum 'struck him down and killed him,' and the biblical writer observes that the word spoken to Jehu, that four generations would sit on the throne, 'was fulfilled,' 2 Kings 15:8-12. 'Isaac' is used here for the northern kingdom, a rare but real way of naming Israel in the prophets, and the name may recall Beersheba, where Isaac had built an altar, Genesis 26:25, and which Amos mentions with the other shrines in 5:5 and 8:14.
context.canonical:
The visions place Amos in a line of intercessors. Abraham negotiates for Sodom, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25. Moses pleads for the people after the golden calf and the LORD 'relented from doing harm,' Exodus 32:11-14; he asks pardon again at Kadesh, and the LORD says 'I have pardoned them as you requested,' Numbers 14:19-20. Psalm 106:23 sums up that role: Moses 'stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath.' Samuel, Jeremiah and Ezekiel know the same standing place, and Ezekiel hears that the LORD 'searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap,' but 'found no one,' Ezekiel 22:30.

The third vision belongs to the same canonical pattern as the end of intercession. In Jeremiah 7:16 the LORD says 'do not pray for these people... for I will not listen to you,' and in Jeremiah 15:1 'Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before Me, My heart would not go out to this people.' Amos does not appear to be forbidden to pray, but the pattern is similar: a time comes when the door of intercession closes. The pairing of patience and limit appears in the prophets in the passage where the LORD explains that He will relent if a nation turns, Jeremiah 18:7-10.

The plumb line gives Scripture a standing image of divine measurement. Isaiah 28:17 has the LORD say 'I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level' as He lays a cornerstone in Zion, 28:16. After the exile, the measuring line turns from demolition to rebuilding: the LORD returns to Jerusalem 'with mercy' and 'a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem,' Zechariah 1:16, and in Zechariah 4:10 the plumb line is in Zerubbabel's hand as the temple is rebuilt. The New Testament ends with an angel holding a golden measuring rod to measure the new city, Revelation 21:15, and Hebrews 7:25 gives the intercessor's role to Christ, who 'always lives to intercede.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Amos put these visions in the book for two audiences. For Israel, they explained why the judgment was coming and why it was just. The people could not say that they had never been given time: twice the LORD had stopped, and the visions show that the delay was the result of a prophet's pleading. They were living on borrowed mercy, and the third vision announced that it was spent.

For the faithful, the visions were meant to show how a prophet should stand. Amos does not defend the nation's innocence. He does not say they deserve the reprieve; he appeals only to their smallness: 'How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?' He stands in the gap as someone who loves the people he is warning, and the book's severity is to be read alongside this. A man who spoke so harshly in public had pleaded for them in private.

Amos also wanted his hearers to understand what kind of God judged them. The visions are given by 'the Lord GOD,' who is addressed in the plea and who answers. This is no distant force. He explains what He is doing, listens when He is addressed, and comes to a conclusion. The plumb line vision, with its question, is a lesson for a prophet who is being brought inside the divine purpose, as Amos 3:7 says the Lord does not act without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what happened in the prophet's visions and what the LORD did in response. It does not promise that any prayer for mercy will cancel a coming judgment. The text records two reprieves, and then a third occasion on which no reprieve is requested or given, and it would be a misreading to take the first two as a formula. What it does commend, by example, is intercession: a prophet who knows that his nation deserves what is coming and still asks God to be merciful. Believers are commanded elsewhere to pray for those in authority, for enemies and for one another, 1 Timothy 2:1-4 and James 5:16-18, and Amos shows what that praying looks like when it is honest about guilt.

The plumb line, too, is descriptive of what God did to Israel, but it teaches a standard that applies to everyone. A wall is true or it is not, and the question of whether we are straight against God's rule does not depend on our feelings. For Christians the answer is not to build a straighter wall by effort, but to look to the one whose life is the standard and to the grace that is able to reset a crooked life. The passage warns against presuming on patience, as Paul warns in Romans 2:4, but it does not teach us that the door of mercy can be measured in advance.

debates.question: What does it mean that the LORD 'relented'?

views.label: A real, relational response, not a change in God's nature
views.case: The verb nacham is used of God responding to intercession and to repentance, as in Exodus 32:14 and Jonah 3:10. Jeremiah 18:7-10 explains the principle: God announces judgment or blessing conditionally, and 'if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster.' On this view, God remains perfectly consistent in being both just and merciful, and the conditions are part of how He works with people.

views.label: Language of appearance, not of change
views.case: Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say that God is not a man that He should 'change His mind.' The same verb that Amos 7:3 uses for the LORD's relenting appears in 1 Samuel 15:29 in the denial that God changes His mind, and in 15:11 for God 'regretting' Saul's kingship. Many interpreters conclude that the language describes how events look from the human side, while God's purposes stand unchanged.

views.label: Both, in different senses
views.case: A third view notes that God is unchanging in His character, purposes and promises, yet He freely enters real relationships in which His actions depend on our responses. The vision cannot mean that the prophet taught God compassion He lacked, nor can it mean that nothing happened. God was moved, and the outcome was different because Amos prayed.

debates.bearing: All three views guard what the passage requires: God's mercy is real and responsive, and His faithfulness is not in doubt. Prayer matters, and the plumb line shows that God's patience has a righteous limit.

debates.question: What is an anak, and is it a plumb line?

views.label: A plumb line
views.case: The traditional reading, followed by the BSB, takes anak as a plumb line or a builder's weight. This suits the context: the Lord stands beside 'a wall true to plumb' and in his hand is the tool that tests the wall. Other passages use plumb lines in judgment, 2 Kings 21:13, Isaiah 28:17.

views.label: Tin
views.case: The word occurs only in Amos 7:7-8 in the Hebrew Bible, which leaves its meaning to be inferred. Some interpreters note a similar word for tin in related languages and suggest that the vision is of a wall of tin, with tin in the Lord's hand. The sense would then be harder to fix, and the explanation in verse 8 would be the key.

debates.bearing: The traditional reading has the best claim, since the vision and its explanation both speak of setting a standard among the people. The oddity of the word is a reminder to hold the details lightly and to attend to the main point: the LORD has measured and found them wanting.

debates.question: Why does Amos not intercede a third time?

views.label: He sees that the limit has come
views.case: The third vision is introduced with a question and ends with 'I will no longer spare them.' Amos is not given the opening to plead. The pattern of two successes followed by a closed door teaches that patience ends.

views.label: Intercession has been forbidden or is futile
views.case: Jeremiah 7:16 and 15:1 give examples where the LORD forbids or refuses prayer for a people. If the same applies here, the silence of Amos is obedience.

debates.bearing: The lesson is the same. The door of mercy stays open as long as God's patience holds, but no one may treat that as a guarantee, and the right response to the third vision is repentance, not a clever plea.

study.originalLanguages:
The first vision begins with a word easy to miss in English. The BSB says the LORD 'was preparing swarms of locusts,' and the Hebrew verb is yotser, from yatsar, the word for a potter forming clay. It is the verb used in Genesis 2:7, 'the LORD God formed the man.' Amos shows the Creator shaping the locust swarm as He once shaped the man, and the careful word makes the plague no accident but a made thing, designed and held under control. Joel calls these locusts 'My great army,' Joel 2:25.

The prophet's first cry is salach, forgive, and his second is different. In verse 5 he says 'please stop,' from chadal, to cease or desist. The first prayer asks for pardon of sin; the second asks only that the judgment stop. Both are petitions to the LORD as 'Lord GOD,' the title that joins Adonai with the covenant name. The cry that follows each, mi yaqum Yaakov, can be rendered 'who will raise up Jacob?' as well as 'how will Jacob survive,' and the verb qum, to rise, takes the reader back to Amos 5:2, 'never to rise again,' and forward to 9:11, where God promises to raise up the fallen tent of David. Amos is already asking the question that the book will eventually answer.

The fire of verse 4 is introduced by a rare phrase, in which the LORD is 'calling' for something by fire. The verb used is the one for a legal dispute, rib, which is the word of the covenant lawsuit. Judgment by fire is God arguing His case. The fire 'consumed the great deep,' tehom rabbah, the same expression as in Genesis 7:11, where the great deep burst forth in the Flood. The writer chooses the language of creation's most primal waters, and the vision says that nothing stands in the way of this fire.

The word anak, plumb line, occurs only here, in verses 7 and 8, in the whole Hebrew Bible, and for that reason its sense must be inferred from the setting. Elsewhere the builder's plumb weight is mishqelet, as in 2 Kings 21:13 and Isaiah 28:17. The Lord 'was standing by a wall,' and nitsav, standing, is the posture of someone who has taken a position and will not move. The LORD 'sets' the line 'among My people,' beqerev, from a word for the inward parts or the midst. God measures Israel from within.

Verse 8 ends with the clause 'I will no longer spare them,' literally 'I will not again pass by him,' using the verb avar. The same verb is used in Micah 7:18 of the God who 'passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance.' In Amos 5:17 it is used for the LORD who will 'pass through your midst' in judgment. Passing over is what the LORD has been doing, and the third vision says He will do it no more.

In verse 9 the sanctuaries of Israel will be 'laid waste,' charab, which sounds like the word for 'sword,' chereb, in the same verse. The ruin of the shrines and the sword are set side by side in sound.

typology.type: Amos pleading, 'How will Jacob survive?' Amos 7:2, 5
typology.fulfillment: Amos stands between God and a guilty nation and obtains a reprieve. He is one of several figures, Abraham, Moses and Samuel among them, who stand in the breach, Psalm 106:23. In Christ the pattern reaches its fullness. He 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25, and He did so by giving His life: He 'bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12. The type falls short because Amos pleaded on the ground of Jacob's smallness and could only delay the judgment, while Christ pleads on the ground of His own blood, Hebrews 9:24, and ends it for His people.

typology.type: The plumb line and the wall, Amos 7:7-8
typology.fulfillment: The LORD measures His people against a standard and finds them crooked. In Isaiah, the measuring line of justice accompanies the laying of a stone in Zion, 'a precious cornerstone,' Isaiah 28:16-17. Peter takes that stone to be Christ, 'the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight,' 1 Peter 2:4-6, and Paul calls Him the cornerstone of the household of God, Ephesians 2:20-22. In Christ the standard and the foundation are the same person: the wall that is true to plumb is the one on which the crooked are rebuilt. The type falls short in that the plumb line in Amos only exposes, while the cornerstone also supports.

typology.type: The measuring line from demolition to rebuilding
typology.fulfillment: The line that the LORD stretches over a city can be used to pull it down, as in 2 Kings 21:13 and Lamentations 2:8, or to mark out its restoration, as in Zechariah 1:16 and Zechariah 2:1-5. The book of Revelation closes with an angel measuring the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:15. The measuring that began as a sign of judgment in Amos finishes as a sign of a secured city. This is a thread of imagery rather than a strict type, but it shows how the same tool carries both the verdict and the promise.

typology.type: The prayer that is not granted, Gethsemane
typology.fulfillment: Amos obtains two reprieves for Israel by asking that judgment pass. In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed, 'let this cup pass from Me,' and then, 'if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done,' Matthew 26:39, 42. The pattern is a contrast. The judgment that Amos's prayers delayed could not be set aside forever, and it fell on the One who prayed for it to pass and then drank it. This is not a prediction in Amos, but the parallel shows why a God who would not spare in the third vision could spare His people at the cross.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by showing the need for a better intercessor. Amos does what he can: twice he asks, and twice the LORD relents. Yet he can only appeal to Jacob's smallness, and a reprieve based on pity cannot change the underlying fact that the wall is crooked. When the third vision comes there is nothing more he can say. The New Testament presents Christ as the intercessor who does not merely request but secures. 'He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25. He is 'at the right hand of God... interceding for us,' Romans 8:34, and we have 'an advocate before the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One,' 1 John 2:1. Where Amos could delay the fire, Christ takes it.

It leads to Christ through the plumb line. The vision shows God testing Israel against His own uprightness, and the verdict is that the wall is not straight. Paul states what every wall must hear: 'There is no distinction, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,' Romans 3:22-23. Jesus alone is 'without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. He is the one life that meets the line, and Paul adds that 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Those who are in Him are no longer measured by their own straightness but by His.

It leads to Christ through the cornerstone. The word that follows the measuring line in Isaiah is 'a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation,' Isaiah 28:16. Peter and Paul identify that cornerstone with Jesus, 1 Peter 2:4-6 and Ephesians 2:20-22. A builder lays the corner first and sets everything else by it. The crooked wall of Israel and the crooked lives of the rest of us are not torn down and discarded but rebuilt on Him, being 'built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22.

It leads to Christ at Gethsemane. The prayer of Amos is answered, and the prayer of Jesus is not: 'let this cup pass from Me' is met by the Father's will that He drink it, Matthew 26:39. The judgment that the prophets feared and sometimes held back falls on the sinless Son so that, as Romans 3:26 says, God may be just and still justify the one who has faith in Jesus.

A caution keeps this honest. Amos 7 does not mention the Messiah, and the plumb line is not a hidden picture of Jesus. The link is made by the larger testimony of Scripture about intercession, the cornerstone and the standard. What Amos gives us is the question the gospel answers: what happens when mercy has been used up, and when the one who pleads can only delay?
study.god:
The visions show a God who is sovereign over creation's smallest and largest forces. He forms the locust swarm, summons the fire and consumes the great deep. Nothing in the chapter happens by chance or by an independent power, and so nothing can be blamed on forces beyond His control. The same sovereignty makes His mercy remarkable. The One who could finish Israel with a swarm stops when a shepherd cries out, and His power is shown as much in restraint as in force.

He is a God who shows His plans. The words 'This is what the Lord GOD showed me' tell us that He brings Amos into the council of what He means to do, as Amos 3:7 puts it, and He asks questions: 'Amos, what do you see?' He might have simply announced the verdict. Instead He draws the prophet into seeing it for himself, and the question invites the answer 'A plumb line' before He explains. The God of the visions engages persons.

He is responsive. The cry of Amos is heard, and the outcome is changed. Scripture puts this beside the affirmation that He is not a man that He should change His mind, Numbers 23:19, using the same verb in 1 Samuel 15:29 that Amos uses of the reprieve. The tension is real, and Scripture holds it without resolving it into a formula. God is unchanging in His character and purposes, yet He enters into relationship in which prayer matters. Jeremiah 18:7-10 shows how the two fit: God's warnings are the means by which He calls people to turn, and His relenting is the faithfulness of One who said He would.

He is just and measures with a standard. The plumb line is not an arbitrary preference but His own uprightness, and there is no judgment by caprice. A wall is straight or it is not, and God does not condemn unfairly. At the same time His mercy extends to the end of what justice allows, and the third vision announces not that mercy has failed but that it has been fully extended. Peter explains the patience behind it: the Lord 'is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance,' 2 Peter 3:9.

He is present in the midst. The line is set 'among My people,' and the Lord stands beside the wall. The same God who dwells with His people is the God who tests them, and nearness does not mean permissiveness. That is a hard truth for people who think of God's presence as a shelter from judgment.

For worship, the chapter asks us to pray boldly and honestly, as Amos does, with an appeal to mercy and without claiming merit, and to treat the patience of God as a gift that we are not entitled to. It also gives us a reason to thank Him that in Christ He has done what no prophet could, for a plumb line that condemns can be borne only by someone who is straight.

crossReferences.note: Abraham bargains with the LORD for Sodom, asking whether He would sweep away the righteous with the wicked. It is the model of the intercession Amos offers, a plea that rests on God's character, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?', and not on the merit of the guilty.

After the golden calf, Moses asks the LORD to turn from His fierce anger, and the LORD relents from the harm He had spoken of. The same verb appears in Amos 7:3 and 7:6, and the pattern of threat, plea and reprieve is the same.

Moses asks pardon for the people on the basis of the greatness of God's loving devotion, and the LORD says 'I have pardoned them as you requested.' It shows what Amos's cry 'forgive' rests on: the character of God, which is greater than the sin of the people.

God explains that He may announce judgment on a nation but 'will relent of the disaster' if it turns from evil, and may announce blessing but relent if it does evil. This gives the principle that makes sense of the relenting in Amos 7: God's warnings are conditional, and they are meant to be heard.

The Glory of Israel 'does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man.' The verb for changing His mind is the one used of the LORD's relenting in Amos 7. The two verses together show that Scripture holds God's constancy and His responsiveness side by side.

The LORD tells Jeremiah, 'do not pray for these people... for I will not listen to you.' It shows that intercession can reach a point where it is no longer received, which helps explain why the third vision of Amos has no plea and no reprieve.

The LORD lays 'a precious cornerstone' in Zion and says 'I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level.' The plumb line of Amos is here joined to the cornerstone, a link the New Testament takes up when it names Christ the stone, 1 Peter 2:4-6.

The LORD will stretch over Jerusalem 'the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab.' The images of Amos 7 are now remembered as the instruments of Samaria's fall, and Judah is told to expect the same.

A man with a measuring line goes to measure Jerusalem, and the LORD promises to be a wall of fire around it. The tool of Amos's judgment is here a tool of promise, and the city that once faced a plumb line will be protected by God Himself.

The fourth vision repeats the question 'Amos, what do you see?' and the verdict 'I will no longer spare them.' It shows that the third vision was not an isolated word but the opening of a sequence that ends in the declaration that the end has come for Israel.

Christ 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near to God through Him. It is the answer to the limits of Amos's intercession: His priesthood is permanent, and His plea does not depend on the changing mood of a nation.
The Lord's slowness is patience, 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.' It states the purpose behind the delays of Amos 7:1-6 and warns that the end of patience will come.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible turns on the relation of mercy and judgment. From Eden, when the LORD clothed the pair He had to send out, to the flood, when He closed the ark on a family He had saved, God has combined patience with a firm no to evil. Amos 7 puts that pattern into three scenes: two reprieves, then a plumb line. It is one of the clearest places where the reader sees that the patience of God is not weakness and that its end is not caprice.

The passage answers a question from earlier in the story: why does God, who has promised never to abandon His people, allow them to be sent away? The answer of the visions is that He has not rushed. Time and again the LORD has held back, and the prophet's pleading has been a means of grace. The exile will not be a surprise or an injustice, and it is not the end of His purposes, for the same book will end with the promise to raise up the fallen tent of David, Amos 9:11. The question 'who will raise up Jacob?' is the question the whole Bible then answers.

It sets up the great intercessor. The prophets stand in the breach and sometimes win a reprieve, but there is always a point at which the wall still stands crooked. The need that Amos cannot meet is the need that Christ meets. He is both the standard, the one true wall, and the cornerstone on which the rest is built. His prayer at Gethsemane does not turn the cup aside, and so the judgment that Israel deserved falls on Him instead, Romans 3:25-26.

The measuring line follows the story's whole path. It is stretched out in judgment over Samaria and Jerusalem, 2 Kings 21:13, then in promise over a rebuilt city, Zechariah 1:16, and finally in the hand of an angel who measures the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:15. The line that Amos saw as a verdict ends as the sign of a city that cannot fall, a home where God dwells with humanity.

In the new creation, no one will need to plead, 'How will Jacob survive?' Hebrews says that Christ lives to intercede for as long as there is need, and Revelation says that in the city there will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The patience of God will have done its work, and the wall that was crooked will have been rebuilt on the Stone He laid.

quiz.q: Why does God relent from sending the locusts and the fire?

options.text: Because the prophet intercedes, pleading forgive, and God genuinely responds in mercy.
options.note: Twice Amos pleads and the LORD relents, showing real responsiveness to prayer.

options.text: Because the threats were never serious to begin with.
options.note: The disasters were real; God truly withheld them at the plea.

options.text: Because God changed His unchanging character.
options.note: God's character does not change; He truly responds within it to intercession.

options.text: Because Amos prayed and God held back the judgment.
options.note: Correct, and the point is that God's mercy is genuinely moved by intercession.

quiz.q: What does the plumb line reveal about Israel?

options.text: Measured against God's own uprightness, Israel is so crooked that the wall must fall.
options.note: The plumb line tests whether a wall is true; Israel is found beyond correction.

options.text: That God is planning some building repairs in Samaria.
options.note: The plumb line is a picture of God measuring His people, not a construction project.

options.text: That Israel has drifted from God's standard.
options.note: Right, and specifically that they are now beyond correction, so judgment will not be spared.

options.text: That God wants to help them straighten out slowly.
options.note: The verdict here is that He will no longer spare them, not a gentle correction.

quiz.q: Why is the third vision different from the first two?

options.text: There is no plea and no relenting; God declares He will spare Israel no longer.
options.note: The pattern of intercession and relenting is broken, marking the limit of patience.

options.text: It involves a bigger natural disaster than the others.
options.note: The difference is not scale but the absence of relenting.

options.text: It moves from mercy withheld to judgment declared.
options.note: Right, and concretely there is no longer any relenting after the plea.

options.text: It is only a dream with no real meaning.
options.note: It is a true vision with a decisive verdict on Israel.

quiz.q: How does Amos the intercessor point to Christ?

options.text: Amos can only plead for pardon; Christ secures it by His blood and ever lives to intercede.
options.note: Christ is the greater mediator who prevails, Hebrews 7:25.

options.text: It simply shows that prayer is a good habit.
options.note: True, but the deeper link is Christ the mediator who obtains what Amos can only ask.

options.text: It shows that other people also prayed for Israel.
options.note: Right that intercession runs through Scripture, but it culminates in Christ.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: The prophet's intercession points directly to Jesus, our intercessor.

quiz.q: What do these visions teach about God's patience?

options.text: His forbearance is real and moved by prayer, yet it has a righteous limit for those who will not be made straight.
options.note: Mercy that truly relents, and justice that finally falls, are held together.

options.text: God's patience never runs out, so judgment is never really coming.
options.note: The plumb line shows patience has a righteous limit.

options.text: God is impatient and quick to destroy.
options.note: The opposite: He relents twice before the verdict falls.

options.text: God is patient but will not overlook persistent, uncorrected sin.
options.note: Right; the passage roots this in the plumb line finding Israel beyond correction.

questions: Amos threw the nation on God's mercy with a single word, forgive. Where do you need to stop pleading your own merit and simply ask God to forgive?
Twice God relented at a prophet's prayer. Who is God calling you to stand in the gap for, trusting that intercession truly moves Him?
The plumb line measures us against God's uprightness, not our own. How do you tend to measure yourself by a lower standard, and what does God's standard reveal?
God's patience is real but not endless. Is there an area where you have presumed on His forbearance rather than letting Him make you straight?
Christ is the intercessor who prevails and the one upright man who bears the judgment of the crooked. How does resting in Him change the way you face God's holy standard?

translationNotes.note: The king's harvest refers to a royal levy on the first mowing; the late spring crop that followed was the people's own food, so the locusts threatened outright famine.
The LORD relented renders nacham; older versions read repented. It describes God genuinely responding to intercession, not a moral change or a mistake corrected.
Plumb line renders the rare word anak, a builder's cord weighted with tin or lead to test whether a wall stands true; the image measures Israel against God's own uprightness.
